newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa rand/bonds closing report.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa rand/bonds closing report.

text.p: The South African rand made further headway against the dollar in thin trading on Thursday, after a weaker start, while bonds took heart from better-than-expected November inflation figures.
The rand finished local trade nearly three cents off the day's low and just under one cent up from Thursday.
Dealers said business was very thin with few corporates showing interest, although there was more enthusiasm for the currency being shown by London banks.
Some dealers reported the Reserve Bank was in the market in the late morning but a central bank spokesman, speaking shortly after midday, denied this.

Forex traders said the rand would remain volatile given the absence of many players which meant a small order could move the market, but said there was no reason to expect any further decisive moves this week.
"I think we'll move sideways now going into the weekend," said one.
Dealers said the rand looked comfortable below 4.70 and it seemed unlikely it would re-test its October 31 record low of 4.7670 bid over the Christmas period, as many had feared last week.
The rand was last trading at 4.6650/6700 on the dollar from a day low of 4.6925/6975 and 4.6730/6780 at 1400 GMT Wednesday.
Against the crosses, it was last at 7.7592/7722 against sterling from 7.8106/8320 and at 0.3344/3349 marks from 0.3317/3325.

Bonds advanced strongly, after a soft start, on the November CPI data. Year-on-year headline inflation came in at 9.2 percent versus the consensus forecast of 9.5 and 9.1 in October. Food was the surprise factor, showing a nil month-on-month rise.
Analysts said this suggested inflation would peak at under 10 percent in December, despite fuel and mortgage rate price hikes this month.
Johan Roussouw, economist at stockbroker Huysamer Stals, predicted a rise in inflation to 9.9 percent in December.
Dealers said the bond market would be looking next at November trade data which the South African Revenue Services aims to release at 0800 GMT on Friday.
South Africa's trade surplus rocketed to 3.9 billion rand in October from 666.7 million rand in September - far exceeding economists' most optimistic forecasts.
Anlaysts are not expecting a repeat of the bumper performance in November, but most hope for a healthy surplus, underlining the country's improving current account position.
The benchmark R150 was yielding 16.12 percent, sharply down on the 16.26 seen before the release of CPI data, and compared to 16.195 percent on Wednesday.
The daily money market shortage rose again to 10.904 billion rand on Wednesday from 10.608 billion rand on Tuesday -- the highest level since April 30.
Three-month NCD rates were steady at 17.40 and 17.75 percent while the 90-day BA rate was also unchanged at a year high of 16.70 to 17.00 percent.
But traders said the bond market appeared to be taking the money market squeeze in its stride.
"Maybe sentiment has changed a little bit. December always sees a cash squeeze but in January it should come down and once the short end eases the long end (yields) can come off too," said one.
Bond Exchange statistics showed foreigners sold a net 128.77 million rand's worth of South African bonds on Wednesday after selling 55.32 million rand's worth on Tuesday.
Nominal cumulative turnover was 3.57 billion rand from 2.21 billion rand.
-- Ben Hirschler, Johannesburg newsroom 27 11 482 1003
